clinician.final_diagnosis: Pellet embolism in right internal carotid artery with thrombus causing acute cerebral infarction
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 13-year-old boy presented with an accidental air rifle chest injury (5 mm entry wound, lower sternum) and stable vital signs initially. Four hours post-admission, he developed neurological symptoms including generalized tonic-clonic seizures, decreased consciousness, left-sided weakness, and contralateral facial weakness. Non-contrast CT brain identified a hyperdense pellet near the right base of the skull adjacent to the carotid canal along with a thrombus in the right middle cerebral artery. Contrast-enhanced CT scan confirmed the pellet embolism lodged in the right internal carotid artery at the carotid foramen, with non-opacification consistent with thrombus causing acute cerebral infarction. Carotid duplex ultrasonography showed turbid flow and obstruction in the right internal carotid artery without dissection. Due to cerebral edema, a decompressive craniotomy was performed. Four-vessel cerebral Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA) was undertaken to assess vasculature and attempt thrombus aspiration; however, the firmly lodged pellet prevented foreign body removal and no cross-circulation was noted from the left ICA. After two weeks of specialized inpatient care, the patient sustained permanent hemiplegia and was transferred to a rehabilitation center.
